analysis.one_liner: Bars corporate lobbyists from federal jobs, bans most official stock trading, and creates a new ethics enforcement agency.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to ten House committees in November 2018 and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul federal ethics and lobbying law. It would bar corporate lobbyists from federal jobs for six years, ban senior officials and Members of Congress from owning or trading individual stocks, require the President and Vice President to disclose tax returns and divest conflicted assets into blind trusts, apply the judicial Code of Conduct to Supreme Court Justices, create a new Office of Public Integrity to enforce the rules, impose a progressive tax on lobbying spending, and extend the Freedom of Information Act to federal contractors. Introduced six weeks before the end of the 115th Congress, it was referred to ten committees and none took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, in the bill's framing: the rules would reduce the movement of officials between government and industry, require officials to disclose their finances and tax returns, and give the public more information about who is lobbying whom. Career federal employees and judges would get clearer conflict-of-interest rules, and litigants would gain a private right to enforce some provisions.

how_it_helps.text: Bars former registered lobbyists from executive branch jobs for two years and former corporate lobbyists for six years, and applies the same bans to congressional staff hires.

Prohibits senior government officials from owning or trading individual stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, derivatives, and hedge fund interests, and extends a full trading ban to Members of Congress and committee staff.
Requires the President, Vice President, and their spouses and minor children to disclose financial interests, divest conflicted interests into blind trusts, and submit three years of tax returns.
Extends public records requirements to federal contractors, requires large contractors to make public disclosures, and strengthens Freedom of Information Act enforcement.
Applies the Code of Conduct for United States Judges to Supreme Court Justices.
Creates an Office of Public Integrity to register and police lobbyists, and bans the hiring of senior executives from companies that settled federal enforcement actions for six years.
Bans bonus and retention payments, or 'golden parachutes,' designed to compensate executives for taking federal jobs, and imposes a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures.
Requires Presidents, Members of Congress, and certain candidates to disclose their personal income tax returns, and extends FOIA to federal contractors for the first time.

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and the corporations they represent, large banks and companies that routinely hire former officials, federal contractors who would face new disclosure and records obligations, and senior officials themselves, who would have to divest individual securities and business holdings, disclose tax returns, and wait longer before cashing in on government service.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lobbying firms, giant banks, contractors, senior officials

drawbacks.text: The divestment rules are sweeping: senior officials at the GS-14 level and above could not own any individual stock, could not keep ownership in privately held businesses except small businesses with under $5 million in receipts, and could not keep conflicted family trusts, which could deter experienced private-sector professionals from entering government.

The hiring and post-employment restrictions are broad: a company could not hire a former senior official from any agency it lobbied in the previous two years, and giant banks and large companies face civil penalties starting at one percent of annual net profit and escalating to five percent for repeat violations, with bans of up to eight years from federal business for violations.

Banning corporate lobbyists from federal posts for six years and taxing lobbying spending could push influence work toward less visible channels, such as unregistered strategic advising, unless the bill's expanded definitions and disclosure rules capture it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core aim — separating government service from personal enrichment and paid influence — addresses a problem that affects everyone, and its harshest rules are aimed at large companies and senior officials rather than ordinary households. The real costs fall on mid-level career employees whose household investments would be restricted, on companies navigating new hiring bans, and possibly on the quality of candidates willing to serve under strict divestment rules. How well the expanded definitions hold up in practice would matter as much as the headline bans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 16, 2018, referred to ten House committees, and none of them scheduled a hearing or markup before the 115th Congress ended six weeks later.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on November 16, 2018, with eight initial cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and nine additional committees, including Oversight and Government Reform, Ways and Means, Financial Services, Rules, and Intelligence.
The complete action history shows only introduction and referral; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms, large companies that hire former officials, and the existing ethics framework's limited enforcement came out ahead, since the rules the bill would have imposed — the lobbyist hiring bans, the official stock-trading ban, the presidential divestment and tax-return requirements, and the contractor disclosure rules — never took effect. Members of Congress were also better off, keeping the current, looser disclosure and trading rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbying firms and the revolving door

sides.party_line_note: All ten initial supporters were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; Republicans held the House majority, and the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill bars corporate lobbyists from government jobs for six years, taxes lobbying expenditures on a progressive scale, bans contingent-fee lobbying and lobbyist campaign contributions, and moves lobbyist registration and enforcement from the Clerk and Secretary of the Senate to a new enforcement office. Its entire business model is paid access to officials, which the bill would restrict and price.

industries.industry: Giant banks and very large corporations
industries.note: Companies over roughly $150 billion in market capitalization and federal contractors with over $5 billion in annual revenue could not hire former senior officials for four years, senior executives of companies that settled federal enforcement actions would be barred from government for six years, and violations of hiring bans would carry penalties starting at one percent of annual net profit. These firms currently use the revolving door as a routine channel of influence.

The bill would subject for-profit federal contractors to the Freedom of Information Act, require public disclosure by large contractors, and bar contractors from hiring the officials who oversaw their contracts for four years. Contractors today operate largely outside public records law.

The bill would amend the Lobbying Disclosure Act and the Internal Revenue Code to require more transparency about the funding and lobbying of 501(c)(6) trade associations and nonprofit groups, channels that currently shield donors and funders from disclosure.

Members of Congress, senior officials, and the President and Vice President would have to divest individual securities and conflicted business interests, disclose tax returns, and face new post-employment income disclosures. The rules bind the people who wrote them, which is why the public benefit runs alongside the burden on officials.
